newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian farmers block airports as milk row grows.
newsitem.headline: Italian farmers block airports as milk row grows.

text.p: Italian farmers blockaded Milan and Venice airports on Friday in a dramatic extension of their protest against tough European Union milk quotas, as talks with the government to resolve the growing crisis ground to a halt.

Dairy farmers, who are fighting to overturn hefty EU fines for milk overproduction, also threatened to block motorways across the north of Italy to force Prime Minister Romano Prodi to accept their demands.
"We are tired and we want to put pressure on the government," the farmers' unofficial leader Aldo Bettinelli told reporters in Milan.
Hundreds of tractors snarled traffic around Venice's Marco Polo airport, while passengers trying to reach Milan's Linate airport were forced to walk the final kilometre to the terminal.
Farmers also sealed roads around Milan's international airport Malpensa, where tractors have been building up all week in preparation for the blockade.
They had shut off Linate airport last week, but opened the roads again on Monday after Prodi promised to hear their grievances.
Prodi said on Friday he would open an inquiry into the contested milk quotas, but the farmers said on Friday that was not enough.
Paolo Micolini, chairman of the small farmers' association Coldiretti, said talks with the centre-left government were now on ice after an inconclusive meeting with Prodi.
"The negotiations have been tough...we have reached no agreement and there were some very tense moments," he told reporters. "Meetings are now suspended even if we are still open to talks."
Bettinelli warned that protesting farmers were also ready to close down motorway exits at the northern cities of Modena, Reggio Emilia and Piacenza, as well as the Parma ring road.
Italian dairy farmers have been hit with some 370 billion lire ($235 million) of fines, which have to be paid by the end of the month, for exceeding milk quotas in the 1995/96 season.
Farmers complain that they have fallen foul of unfair EU rules which allow them to produce just 9.9 million tonnes of milk a year against Italy's total milk consumption of some 18 million tonnes.
The government has asked Brussels to increase the Italian quotas, but in the meantime has said farmers must pay the fines themselves.
Some 14,834 dairy farmers, mainly in the north of the country, have received fines, with one producer alone facing a one billion lire levy.
The government has offered the farmers cheap loans to tide them over.
